newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy car sector still in slow lane but rally seen.
newsitem.headline: Italy car sector still in slow lane but rally seen.

text.p: Italy's car market was still crawling along in the slow lane in January despite government incentives to boost sales, but dealers and analysts expect the sector to shift into higher gear soon.

The Transport Ministry reported on Monday that 207,000 new cars were registered in January, a modest increase of 4.38 percent on the same month in 1996 but higher than the 111,000 units registered in December 1996.
The Italian car makers' association Anfia said car demand seemed to have started 1997 well after near stagnation in 1996.
"The rise in January, while slight, none the less appears to be the first real symptom of improvement after a long period of depression which began in 1993," Anfia said in a statement.
The government introduced a scheme at the start of the year to coax the market out of depression, offering cash bonuses to motorists to scrap cars more than 10 years old and buy new ones.
The incentives have barely worked their way into January data but analysts say, judging from order flows, February and successive months will see much stronger growth.

"We know because of the incentives February is going to be a monster month and there will be several more frisky months afterwards," said John Lawson, automotive analyst at Salomon Brothers in London.

Leading sector researcher CSP said in a statement the impact of the scheme on January registrations was practically nil even though it estimated that orders for new cars rose 33 percent on January 1996 to 255,000.
"This notable volume will be reflected in deliveries in the next few months when the vehicles which have been ordered are available," CSP said.
Car giant Fiat's registrations rose 1.09 percent to 93,030 units, but its market share was slightly down at 44.95 percent, from 46.40 percent a year ago.
On the whole car dealers were much more positive than previously about the outlook for their market.
"At the end of January the percentage of dealers expecting a high level of orders coming in rose to 65 percent from 30 percent in December and six percent in September," CSP said.
More than 60 percent expected orders to grow in the coming months and dealers were even starting to show concern over the possibility of satisfying the high level of demand promptly.
"In January there were signs of a perceptible change in stocks of new cars and for the next few months a further contraction in car availability is expected," CSP said.
Behind the effect of the incentives, CSP said a mild recovery in Italy's sluggish market was continuing, although Anfia noted the figures were still down on 1993 and 1992.

Lawson said considerable pent-up demand for new vehicles existed in Italy but consumer incomes were not growing enough to release that demand. Introduction of incentives was likely to prove the trigger at least for the nine months the scheme lasts.
"The key is whether you attract new customers -- people who would not otherwise have bought a new car -- or whether you are just encouraging people to bring forward their purchase pattern," he said.
